questions.stem: A student places potato chips in different concentrations of salt solution and measures their mass change. In distilled water, the chips gain mass. In concentrated salt solution, they lose mass. What explains the mass loss in salt solution?

options.text: Salt moves into the potato cells by diffusion
Water moves out of the potato cells by osmosis to the more concentrated solution
The potato cells absorb salt and become heavier
The potato dissolves in the salt solution

questions.explanation: Osmosis is the movement of water molecules from a dilute solution (inside the potato cells) to a more concentrated solution (the salt solution) through the partially permeable cell membrane. This net loss of water causes the cells to shrink (plasmolyse) and the potato chip to lose mass and become flaccid.

questions.stem: Red blood cells are placed in pure water and they burst (lyse). However, plant cells placed in pure water do not burst. Why?

options.text: Plant cells do not take in water by osmosis
The rigid cell wall of plant cells prevents them from bursting
Plant cells have smaller vacuoles than animal cells
Red blood cells have a larger surface area

questions.explanation: In pure water (hypotonic solution), water enters both cell types by osmosis. Animal cells have no cell wall, so they swell and burst. Plant cells also swell, but the rigid cellulose cell wall prevents over-expansion. The cell becomes turgid (firm) as pressure builds up, which actually helps support the plant.

questions.stem: A gardener accidentally uses too much fertiliser on their plants. The plants wilt despite the soil being moist. What has happened?

options.text: The fertiliser has blocked the stomata
The soil solution is now more concentrated than the root cell sap, so water moves out of the roots by osmosis
The fertiliser has killed all the bacteria in the soil
The plants are absorbing too much water

questions.explanation: Excess fertiliser makes the soil solution very concentrated (hypertonic to the root cells). Water moves out of the root cells by osmosis, down the water potential gradient. This causes the root cells to become plasmolysed and the plant wilts. This is sometimes called 'fertiliser burn'.

questions.stem: In a hospital, patients receiving an intravenous drip are given saline (0.9% salt solution) rather than pure water. Why?

options.text: Salt provides energy for the patient
Pure water would cause red blood cells to take in water by osmosis and burst
Salt kills bacteria in the blood
Pure water cannot flow through IV tubes

questions.explanation: Normal saline (0.9% NaCl) is isotonic with blood -- it has the same concentration as blood plasma. If pure water were injected, it would be hypotonic to the blood cells, causing water to enter by osmosis, making the cells swell and potentially burst (haemolysis). This could be life-threatening.

questions.stem: In the potato osmosis experiment, at one particular concentration of sucrose solution, the potato chip shows no change in mass. What does this concentration represent?

options.text: The concentration at which all osmosis stops permanently
The concentration that is isotonic to the potato cell contents
The point where active transport takes over from osmosis
The concentration where the potato becomes fully turgid

questions.explanation: When there is no change in mass, the external solution has the same water potential (is isotonic to) the cell contents. Water molecules still move in both directions by osmosis, but the rate in equals the rate out, so there is no net movement of water and no change in mass.
